projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert C. Walton was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Robert C. Walton. Mr. Walton served in the U.S. Army Air Corps with the 13th Air Force, 64th Troop Carrier Squadron He served in the Pacific Theatre, and his highest rank was first sergeant. I am Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Walton's home in Willoughby, Ohio, on September 18, 2003. Bob was 83 at the time of this recording

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Let's see, in Lakewood on Newman Avenue, Lakewood, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: I was 21 and eight months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, were you working at that point?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: I think I was on the road with some fellows down at an Ohio State football game, halfway down to Columbus, and that's when we heard about Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Heard it on the car radio?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction, you and the rest of the guys, when you heard that?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: You know, we didn't know the implications, what it was going to be at that time, you know, it was too much information to absorb at that time. I really can't tell you what my reaction was at the time, I don't think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did any of the group decide to run out there and sign up?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Not that I know of. There were three or four of us in the car, you know. And then I was drafted in January 24th.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Forty-two?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah. Right after that -- you want to know what happened after that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure. When you did you report? Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: I reported, and I went to Camp Perry for basic; and from there I was transferred to Jefferson Barracks, Missouri, right on the Missouri River. And we lived in a place called Skunk Hollow, we were living in tents. And we had an epidemic of spinal meningitis, so everybody was quarantined, couldn't go to town, St. Louis, or anything like that. And if a time span of ten days would go by and there were no new cases, then they'd lift of the quarantine. Seemed like always on the ninth day in the middle of the night an ambulance would roll up and take a guy out; some of them died very quickly after that. So this one time I had a call from the Statler Hotel. It was Arlene and her girlfriend calling. So I thought they were calling from the Statler in Cleveland; so, I placed a call there and they knew nothing about that. So then I thought it was St. Louis. Sure enough, that's where they were. They came to visit me. So I went to the first sergeant and I said, "Is there any chance of getting a pass out?" This was a Saturday. He said, "You know we're under quarantine, we aren't giving any passes." He says, "I'll make an exception, I'll let you have a pass, as long as you're back here by 11 o'clock." Okay. So I went into town. Well, trying to make connections back to town -- back from town back to the camp, I didn't get in until 1:30. Then he said, "Well, you're on KP for two weeks now because you didn't know do what you were supposed to do." So, I reported for KP at 3:00 o'clock in the morning, and the mess sergeant says, "You can't go on KP, you've already been assigned to Casey Jones Aeronautical School in Newark, New Jersey, and you're shipping out in two days." That was a good break there, you know, making $21 a month as a private. Get to Newark, New Jersey in the barracks there, and the captain said: "Now, you fellows will be going to school here. We're going to march through town every morning on the way to class. We want you to have a good haircut and your clothes clean and everything, so you're going to get $75 a month instead of $21." So I was there for about eight or nine weeks, and then graduated from that -- it was a mechanics school, Casey Jones Aeronautical School. And I -- So from there I was transferred to Lockboard Air Base in Columbus after I graduated. The crew chief said, "You're supposed to go on a flight." We had C-47s. "You're supposed to go on a flight today but I'll tell you what, I'll go today and you go tomorrow. And I'll take your books, I'd like to see what they're using, regular army manual, you know, see what they're teaching in aeronautical school these days." I said, "Okay." The plane exploded over Columbus, 11,000 feet. I lost all my notes and everything. Of course, he lost his life, and a couple of other members of the crew too. So that was really a tough -- you know, at the time I didn't think anything of it. Later on, wow, that was a close call, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they ever figure out what caused it to explode?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: No. 11,000 feet right over Columbus, Lockboard Air Base is right there. They used to take us into the Ohio State football games in big trucks, you know, to see the games. So that was kind of a nice thing to have to experience. So, from there I was transferred down to Fort Bragg to an outfit down there that was ready to go overseas to Germany, and I was what they call supernumerary. There was eight of us; in case some fellow can't make it, we filled in. Well, so far I escaped that. Somehow I lucked out all the time, you know. So that outfit over there, I was assigned to the 64th Troop Carrier Squadron in Alliance, Nebraska. And we didn't have any planes yet, we had all the personnel but we didn't have planes yet. So we went from, whatever, whatever we were supposed to -- I was supposed to work on the line as a mechanic, and they put me in the intelligence department. And then after I was in there for a while, they put me in the office working there. So, I never had any experience, I only had eighth grade typing, you know, but I started to practice my typing so I could do payroll, you know. And the guys were going into town, I was practicing my typing, everything like that. So that outfit then, finally we got the planes and we were preparing to -- to go overseas, and we got -- went to California; departed from there to New Caledonia, and we were there for a while; and then New Hebrides; and finally to an island along Guatalcanal, the Guadalcanal. We weren't active militarily-wise, but our camp was always at the end of the runways. The C-47's would land and the personnel were there. We had 12 planes, so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About when was it that you want to Guadalcanal?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: That would have been -- well, let's see, I was in the states for 18 months, so that would have been '42, '43, middle of '43, something like that. So then we were on this Island of Biak. No, we were going to go over to this Island of Biak, which is right off the end of Guadalcanal. And, of course, everybody, the personnel was over there. We found out there -- the fellows were starting to die there. There were a coonig (ph) grass growing there, and the rats gets in there with chicks, get on the guys and they'd die in about ten days. So they flew everybody off that island, put them back on the Guadalcanal, and all the clothing was impregnated with a chemical, and we went back there and that's where we had our base at that time. But preparatory before the whole outfit went there, they sent me over with 45 men, I was supposed to be in charge of 45 men, and we had to clean the island so the growth, jungle growth, it was all coral underneath and get natives to build frames of tents and all that sort of thing. Because we because we had 265 enlisted men and 100 officers, flying personnel, not only flyers but navigators, radio operators, things like that. So it turned out that after we were there, the rest of the organization joined us. They had an old regular army maquista (ph), my first sergeant; he was a rough old guy, nobody liked him. So they got rid of him and made me a first sergeant. So here I am, became first sergeant of the outfit; got along good. Officers wrote to me later and said: "Boy, did things calm down after you took over." Well, I kept things under control myself. I didn't let everything out that probably should have reported it. One time in the middle of the night at the end of the tent, in my tent down at the end of the row there was a disturbance. And I walked over there and here's one of the older guys in the tent, he held up this entire body with a gun. And they were scared to death, they didn't want to make a move. And I didn't know what was going on. I just walked in there, "Give me the gun, man;" just like that, gave me the gun. That was the end of it. I should have reported it, I never did. So, we had our mission there, the planes would fly: Evacuation of the wounded, dropped supplies over the jungles, whatever had to be done. I was at Midway, at Iwo Jima, islands of that kind. And those planes didn't have any ammunition or fire power, you know, or any protection whatsoever, but they used to fly low right down above the water. And then --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job with the outfit?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: I was first sergeant at that time, first sergeant.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: With the flight crew or ground crew or --

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah, the base, you know. Well, the crew would have a navigator, a pilot -- two pilots, and a crew chief, and that's on the planes, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: I never flew, I never worked on a plane one day, never had guard duty one day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what did you do?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Never had KP one day, I lucked out of all that stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I guess.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: So then we got rest leave down in Australia. Because the planes used to fly and the officers would get a rest leave after certain flights, and we'd fly down to Australia. And then they would come back with some -- whatever they could pick up there. One time we had a whole C-47 full of cucumbers, bringing back, you know, things like that. So I was down there for 10 days for rest leave; and rejoined the outfit, and mustered out after a while, you know. My tour of duty with somewhat uneventful as far as any danger is concerned. I mean, there would be Japanese just sitting in the theatre at night on the barrels, you know. I've got a book, I don't know if you'd be interested in seeing the book here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: I'll bring it. We had this second lieutenant who he got all the information ready for this book, had it published down in Australia. And it's a nice book, and not many outfits had things like that, you know. But you know my outfit --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Each group had four squadrons, we were the 64th Squadron; see?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: 403rd, yeah, we were known as the Jungle Air Force. This is -- this is our --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you started to say that when you were in the movie theatre, the Japanese would come into that theatre?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Well, they'd hide in the woods and they, you know, looking for food; see?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: It would be like, let's see, show you more closely. Well, here's Guadalcanal. Here's this Island of Biak, right here. Case so big that you could move a two-family into the scale of that. The Japanese were holed up in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were they still holed up in there when you got there?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Oh, yeah, sure. This is the C-47, that's what we had. We were in the 13th Air Force, in the 13th Air Force. Here's the commander of the 403rd Troop Carrier group. This is captain of the 64th. There was 63, 64, 65 and 66, four squadrons; each one had 12 planes, and they show some of the activities here. We had a fellow that was an artist for Disney, and he painted these, he designed and painted on the planes. See when these planes would go to these islands, there was no place for them to stay. So they set up under -- a mat underneath, and they'd sleep on the ground underneath the plane until it was time to come back. This one, this is what I would have been doing had I continued to be a mechanic on the line. The mission was to keep those 12 planes flying, that was the whole mission; not only the mission itself, but the ground personnel is to keep the planes flying, in operation. This is activities, things, load the planes with supplies. This is Guadalcanal, where we were, right on the ocean. This is evacuation of the wounded.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you eventually moved on to the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah. I went to Leyte in the Philippines. That was the time in the Philippines and the war was over. Here's this Island of Biak and a big poem about it. It's not the greatest place in the world but we spent a whole year there. After we were there for a while, we were -- we were there for over a year, it became pretty established and we were able to construct a enlisted men's hall and officers' hall. And anything that you wanted for that you had to get from the Seabees. And to get anything from the Seabees you had to bribe with a quart of vodka of something that the officers would bring back from Australia. Then we had a basketball court. This isn't going to show much on here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, now that you mention it, they'd take a picture.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: This is our tent area. This is where we clean all the coral free of jungle growth. This is the enlisted men's area. Here's the officers' area. Here's the mess hall. And here's the water tank down here. I can't quite see it, my eyesight is not so good. But you had a water tank, for the guys to take a shower they had go to the Seabees and bribe them. Now, my tent was right here. And that little incident with that fellow with the gun was down here, so I walked down through here; and this was like the middle of the night, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that a case of stress or fatigue for that guy?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah. Mostly fellows that were older, like 42, 43 years old, we had a few of those and they couldn't cope, you know. We were talking about the barrels, sitting on the barrels, we'd sit on those barrels. It used to rain everyday, coming in in the morning the barrels would all float down to the front. So if you want to watch a movie at night, you had to get them back in the place and sit down. But you sit there for -- you only had four films for a month, so you see the same thing over and over again; but, there was nothing else to do. And once in a while a Jap would sneak in from over in the woods area and fire a few shots, because he was looking for food, you know. That's about it, all the officers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any memorable movies from that theatre?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: There was one with Dick Haymes, I think was one. I can't think of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything you got really sick of watching?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: There was nothing else to do, that was the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you could probably do the dialogue along with them; right?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah. Well, not now I couldn't. We lived on Newman Avenue in Lakewood before when I went into the service; right there, Newman Avenue, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get any shows, any USO shows or anything where you were?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We saw Bob Hope several times. He'd have, say, a 7:30, program that's going to start at 7:30, you'd get there at 4:00 in the afternoon. And after it was all over, we got the snoop plane, it was a C-52. That was a Commando. His front would open up and you could drive a Jeep right up into there. That was what we had before. It's a good book, not many --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else from the Bob Hope shows you remember?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Long time ago.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about mail call, did you get packages mailed from home?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah, we did. That was no problem with that. Yeah, those shows was a high point. Bob Hope would come, I forget some of the other entertainers would come through. Frances Langford, she used to sing, she'd always accompany him. He'd have a couple of dancers, you know, things like that. That was routine, that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, they continued to find Japanese on that island right up to the end of the war?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Well, there'd be stragglers here and there, you know, there holed up. I wouldn't be surprised if there was still some in one of those islands hiding away, don't even know the war's over yet, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I remember hearing stories that even in the '60s they were finding people there on those little islands.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah. But after, you know, two and a half years overseas and responsibilities and things that you had there, it was time to go home, and this was in December. As a matter of fact, I got home like New Year's Eve. They put you on these old converter Liberty ships. Because the guys were on that ship, they would give -- they didn't care what your rank was or anything, they'd give you the dirtiest jobs. I was hauling garage out on a scow, dumping it out there, stuff like that, you know? Of course, you didn't care because you were going home. But it was 27 days on the water, and the bunks were all constructed with two-by-fours, seven high, top guy has his nose about a foot from the ceiling there, you know. A couple days out the nails, spikes would come loose and start to creak and things like that, you know. And you had ground meat for 27 days, every meal. They kept it up in a big freezer and it was all frozen hard. And the mess chief would come in with an ax, chop up a big chunk of ground meat, and prepare it some way or the other, you know. That was -- but that's the way it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with -- were you married at the time?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: No, we got married after I got out of the service.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with her and your family like when you got back?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Well, we were -- she had had a stroke when she was 29 years old. She lived close to 112 off of Clifton Boulevard. On a Sunday evening her mother had heard her crying upstairs, and she went up there and she was paralyzed, her whole side was paralyzed for a year. At that time they didn't know what it was or what to do about it. But anyway she was starting to recover and she could walk very slowly. So she and her father and mother came down to get me at the terminal tower down there, and it would take her over a half hour just to walk across that expanse. She had to walk real slow; see? And then we were invited to a New Year's Eve party right after that. And then once we got married, we had four -- four children. They all lived there on 177th. The oldest son Russ has an accounting business. Most PTs, just accounting business in Lake County. He has a lot of good clients. Went on a journey to audit some books for one of his clients by a factory over there. That was a good experience. My second son, Cliff, he's head football coach at Hawkins School. He's been there 25 years. We go to all the Hawkins football games because he had three sons, watched them play, although one's still playing in college but the other two have graduated. And Beverly married Dale Stedner (ph), who lived on 176th, you know, the Salvation Army, that field is in Grovewood and 177th, next street over. But dale lived on that corner, and Beverly met him. She graduated Miami University, and they got married. And he has a catering business in a party center, the Curlander on 306, Dale Stedner. There's my son Bill, he's been divorced twice. He stays with -- that's why this is here. He doesn't want to own anything. He's smart. He can do plumbing, locksmith, electrical, anything, fix it. Because if some companies have trouble with a piece of equipment and the manufacturer sends a rep out to repair it, he can't do it, he calls Bill, and he gets it fixed in five minutes. But he doesn't own anything. This? That's his corner over there with all his stuff, and his golf clubs and he has a van and his tools and things. That's all he owns, he doesn't want anything more than. If he has $200, he's gotta spend it. If he has ten cents in his pocket, doesn't bother him. That's the way he is, just the opposite of the other kids, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during the war, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Well, other than what I already told you, close call and the plane explosion, that was kind of scary. I thought more about that later than I did at the time. I don't even think I told my father and mother about that. They would have been upset about that. Then when I came back from the service -- my father had a heart condition, he couldn't work. He was also an alcoholic, and so they'd move around from different places. I finally rented a farmhouse out at Cherry Valley and moved them out there. Every two weeks I went out there for ten years and took them shopping for food, because they didn't have a car or anything; took care of them. But I'd drive over there Saturday morning every two weeks. It took a good hour to drive out there, Route 6 all the way to Cherry Valley. But they liked it out there because there was a country store right across the street from them, and they were practically on the corner of City Hall there where City Hall is now. There's a big church on that corner, wide open, you know City Hall here, country store here, and then the house that they lived in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Backtracking a bit, do you remember when you heard the news that they dropped the bomb?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Well, somewhat, yeah. They probably showed a newspaper for the troops there. Let's see. There's some newspaper things that I received. This is when we first got the news of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was this just a little camp paper?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah, August 1945.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any wild celebrations on D Day?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah, but there was nothing going on at that time. I had applied for pilot training, I passed everything. Had to have an operation on my nose. Then in Guadalcanal I had had a deviated septum in my nose and they said: "If you're flying at higher altitudes it affects your breathing, so we recommend that you have that taken care of." So they arranged it, and in a tent in Guadalcanal this doctor operated, cut that out. And I could just feel that -- put a chisel up in there, and the last part he had to twist it to get it out. Boy, that hurt. And they packed it with packing. Then the next morning here was all the packing and everything was on the ground. And but then the war was over, which I was thankful for that, but I was due to go for pilot training. It's a good thing I didn't get it though because I have a very bad sense of direction, I would have gotten lost over there. D Day, you've probably seen a lot of this stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I got a copy of that stuff.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah. This is all. But, like I say, aside from that, that's about as much as we had there. Everybody was happy about it and all that because it meant more than anything else there wouldn't be any more casualties and a chance to go home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: I was 15. We didn't have this. I mean I acquired this afterwards. So, that's about -- that's about all I have. But didn't tell you any great experiences or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It's all part of the story.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: But we lived in tents most of the time until we got to those Quonset huts. And we were always at the end of the runway, and these bombers would take off like 3:00 o'clock in the morning, right over our tent, 15 or 20 of them right over the top of that tent; and go like this, every morning, taking off, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. Very good. Do you think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: That's about it, I guess, not a very illustrious story.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But it's all a part of the big story.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Walton
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: We want to hear from everybody that went through it. (END OF CD)
